title: Milky Way
conditions: A clear dark sky, with the bright galactic region above the local horizon and no strong moonlight washing it out. Visibility depends on date, latitude and hemisphere.
intent: A recognisable Milky Way over a simple foreground, with stars close to points.

setup.focusTarget: Magnify a bright star in live view and turn the focus ring until its core is smallest. Check centre and corner stars in an enlarged recorded frame.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start at 10 s. Use the star estimator with actual focal length and pixel pitch. Shorten if stars stretch; raise ISO before extending a motion-limited shutter.

phone.mode: Astrophotography/night mode if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Automatic stack; 5–10 s only in a supported manual app
phone.focus: Lock distant focus and inspect an enlarged frame.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Clamp the main camera and let a supported astro mode finish its sequence. Include a clean distant foreground edge.
phone.limitation: Night-mode duration often describes a stack, not one exposure. Manual ISO, focus and RAW depend on the phone and app.
why: A dark location and a visible galactic band matter more than a long countdown; the phone cannot recover a Milky Way hidden by bright sky.
The main camera is usually the most dependable phone lens in low light; digital zoom enlarges noise without collecting more starlight.
A supported astro mode combines frames while managing star movement. Its total capture duration is not a single shutter setting.
With a fixed aperture, the useful controls are capture mode, support, focus and any genuine shutter/ISO adjustments the app provides.
steps: Check local darkness, clouds, Moon position and galactic visibility for your date, latitude and hemisphere; choose a safe viewpoint before dark.
Clean the main lens, clamp the phone and include a simple distant foreground below the band.
Select astrophotography mode if supported, otherwise try a tripod night capture. Use a manual app only after checking its actual exposure and focus capabilities.
Focus on a bright star using magnification and manual focus if available; otherwise lock focus on a distant light and verify the stars in a recorded test.
Start with the timer and leave the phone untouched until capture and processing finish.

Enlarge centre and corner stars. Correct focus for round swollen stars; in a manual app shorten individual exposures for trails and raise ISO only as needed. Compare a shorter available night capture if the stack smears detail.

essential: Phone with a usable night or astro capture mode
optional: Power bank for a long session

problems.symptom: The sky is bright but no galactic band appears
problems.cause: Moonlight, light pollution or the band being below the horizon
problems.fix: Check local sky position and move to darker conditions or a better date; a longer capture alone will not reveal an absent band.

problems.cause: Incorrect focus, condensation or a dirty lens
problems.fix: Clean and dry the lens, lock distant focus again and inspect an enlarged recorded star.

problems.symptom: Stars become lines or doubled marks
problems.cause: Individual exposures are too long, the phone moved, or the stack failed to align
problems.fix: Secure the clamp; use supported astro capture, or shorten individual exposures in a capable manual app and retest.

problems.symptom: The foreground becomes waxy or patchy
problems.cause: Heavy processing of very dark ground
problems.fix: Use a clear silhouette or make a separate foreground capture for a disclosed blend; avoid forcing noisy shadows bright.

phone.tip: Check one recorded star at high magnification before committing to a long astro sequence; a bright phone preview can hide missed focus.

why: Earth rotation limits the shutter even when the tripod is perfectly still.
A wide aperture gathers faint sky light while a wide field includes the galactic band.
A distant foreground may work at star focus; a nearby object can require a separately focused frame.
Fixed white balance keeps a sequence consistent; RAW retains colour-adjustment freedom.
steps: Check clouds, Moon position, darkness and galactic visibility for the exact location and date.
Choose a safe foreground in daylight and keep lamps out of the composition.
Secure the tripod, select RAW and focus manually on a magnified star.
Take the 10 s test and enlarge stars at the centre and corners.
Shorten shutter for directional trails; refocus round swollen stars; stop down slightly for wing-shaped corner aberrations.
If a near foreground is unsharp, make a separately focused frame and disclose any later blend.

problems.cause: Earth rotation during the exposure
problems.fix: Shorten shutter and raise ISO to restore brightness.

problems.cause: Focus error or dew
problems.fix: Refocus under magnification and inspect the front element.

problems.cause: Wide-open lens aberrations
problems.fix: Try f/3.2–4 and raise ISO while preserving shutter time.

problems.cause: Light pollution or strong moonlight
problems.fix: Change location, direction or timing; avoid exposing the sky into clipping.

alternatives.name: Fast wide lens
alternatives.effect: Similar brightness with less star movement, but possibly softer corners.
alternatives.requirements: An f/1.8 lens and careful corner inspection.

alternatives.name: Tracked sky
alternatives.effect: More sky signal while following star motion.
alternatives.requirements: Accurately aligned tracker; stationary foreground needs a separate capture and disclosed blend.

tip: Check corners as well as the centre: one sharp central star does not prove the whole wide-open frame is clean.
startingPoint: Test star shape in the recorded image before judging brightness. The listed exposure assumes a dark sky.

title: Pinpoint stars and constellations
conditions: A clear night with a recognisable constellation framed more tightly than a whole-sky nightscape.
intent: Small star points, visible star colour and a readable constellation pattern.

setup.focusTarget: Magnify a moderately bright star and minimise its diameter. Verify several recorded stars, not only the live view.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: At 50 mm start at 4 s and test. Pixel pitch, actual focal length, aperture and declination affect the limit; a wide-angle shutter cannot simply be reused.

phone.mode: Night mode or supported manual mode
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Lock focus on a distant light or star.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Use the main camera and a small landmark to establish direction. Reduce exposure if bright stars lose their colour.
phone.limitation: Digital zoom does not replace optical reach; computational smoothing may remove faint stars.
why: Recognisable spacing between the brightest stars matters more than filling the screen with a digitally enlarged pattern.
A stable main-camera capture usually retains more faint stars than an unsupported low-light telephoto view.
Reducing excessive brightness preserves star colour; the phone's aperture is usually fixed, so use exposure adjustment or supported manual controls.
steps: Locate the constellation in a local sky map and confirm that its important stars clear buildings and trees.
Support the main camera and frame the complete pattern with a small distant landmark if useful.
Use supported astro/night capture. If testing optical telephoto, confirm that the app actually uses that camera and supports the required low-light mode.
Lock focus on a distant light or use magnified manual focusing on a star when available, then make a timed test capture.
Enlarge the stars and compare their shape and colour; reduce exposure if the bright ones are featureless, and shorten a genuine manual exposure if they trail.
Save a wider clean frame before cropping; stop enlarging when the pattern becomes noisy rather than clearer.

problems.cause: Heavy digital zoom or insufficient sky signal
problems.fix: Return to the main camera, work under a darker sky and use a supported tripod astro/night mode.

problems.symptom: Bright stars are large white spots
problems.cause: Clipping or inaccurate focus
problems.fix: Reduce capture brightness, verify distant focus and compare an enlarged test before changing both at once.

problems.cause: Noise reduction treats small points as noise
problems.fix: Compare a supported RAW/manual capture or a dedicated astro mode; avoid heavy smoothing in the final edit.

problems.symptom: All stars have matching short streaks
problems.cause: Star movement during individual exposures or movement of the phone
problems.fix: Check the clamp; use shorter genuine manual exposures if supported, and inspect the recorded result rather than relying on the countdown.

phone.tip: Keep the brightest stars of the whole pattern in the frame; a clear constellation is more useful than a large but incomplete crop.

why: A tighter field magnifies star motion, so the exposure is shorter than a wide nightscape.
A wide aperture helps keep the shutter short without excessive ISO.
Preserving bright-star highlights retains more colour than exposing every star to white.
steps: Use a local sky map to locate the pattern above obstructions.
Frame with enough margin to keep its geometry readable.
Manually focus on a magnified star and make a 4 s frame.
Inspect bright and faint stars at enlarged view.
Halve the shutter and double ISO for trails; lower exposure if bright stars clip.

essential: Fast normal or short telephoto lens

problems.cause: Saturated highlights
problems.fix: Reduce ISO or exposure time.

problems.cause: Exposure too long
problems.fix: Shorten shutter and recheck; autofocus is not the cause.

problems.cause: Field curvature, lens alignment or focus placement
problems.fix: Refocus, compare a smaller aperture and inspect the lens setup.

problems.cause: Frame includes too many unrelated stars
problems.fix: Tighten the composition around the recognisable geometry.

alternatives.name: Shorter trail tolerance
alternatives.effect: Less star movement with more ISO noise.
alternatives.requirements: Useful near the celestial equator or at higher pixel density.

alternatives.name: Short-frame stack
alternatives.effect: Aligned frames can reduce noise without lengthening each exposure.
alternatives.requirements: Capture 20–50 matching RAW frames and use star-alignment software.

tip: A medium-bright star is often easier to focus than a saturated one whose bloated core hides the sharpest point.
startingPoint: Enlarge a recorded frame: focal length and output size decide whether four seconds is short enough.

title: Star trails
conditions: A clear night with a fixed foreground and at least half an hour available for consecutive exposures.
intent: Continuous star arcs around a celestial pole or broad sweeps away from it.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a magnified star, inspect a test frame and leave manual focus unchanged for the sequence.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Each 20 s frame belongs to a 30–90 minute sequence. Adjust ISO for sky brightness, minimise gaps and disable long-exposure dark-frame subtraction during the sequence.

phone.mode: Dedicated trail or interval app if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Repeated exposures controlled by the app
phone.focus: Lock focus and exposure before starting.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Clamp the phone and use a true star-trail mode or save individual frames for later blending.
phone.limitation: Normal night mode usually aligns stars and suppresses trails; it is not equivalent to a trail mode.
why: A dedicated trail mode accumulates star movement; an ordinary astro mode may align that movement away.
Total sequence duration determines arc length, while individual-frame brightness determines whether the sky washes out.
An unchanged camera position, distant focus and short capture gaps keep the arcs continuous around the local celestial pole.
steps: Before travelling, verify that the phone offers a real star-trail mode or an interval app that saves frames for later lighten blending.
Choose a safe fixed foreground and the appropriate celestial-pole direction for your hemisphere, or point elsewhere for sweeping arcs.
Clamp the phone securely, lock distant focus on a star or far light, and fix exposure/white balance if the app permits.
Make a short trial sequence and inspect a saved frame for focus and a sky that is not clipped.
Capture a continuous sequence for roughly 30–90 minutes when battery, weather and storage permit; minimise gaps without disturbing the phone.
Review the trail composite or blend the saved frames, checking for jumps, gaps and changing focus before attempting a longer sequence.

essential: Phone with a verified trail mode or interval capture route
optional: Power bank connected before the sequence
Trail-blending software if saving individual frames

problems.symptom: The result has star points instead of trails
problems.cause: Normal astro/night processing aligned the stars
problems.fix: Use a dedicated trail mode or save separate frames and blend without aligning away the sky's movement.

problems.cause: Capture pauses, processing delays or the app being suspended
problems.fix: Use the shortest supported interval gap and a capture app that remains active; test continuity before the full session.

problems.cause: The clamp moved or the phone switched cameras
problems.fix: Secure the mount and keep one physical camera and zoom setting for the entire sequence.

problems.symptom: Trails become thick and hazy later
problems.cause: Condensation or a change in focus
problems.fix: End the sequence, inspect the lens and restore distant focus before starting a new complete sequence.

phone.tip: Keep a clean foreground frame before starting; a passing torch can spoil the ground even when the sky sequence works.

why: Total sequence duration sets trail length; each frame’s exposure controls sky brightness.
Fixed focus, framing and white balance prevent discontinuities.
Long inter-frame gaps create dotted trails, especially with automatic dark frames.
The celestial-pole direction differs by hemisphere; pointing away creates sweeping arcs.
steps: Choose a pole-centred or sweeping-arc composition for the local sky.
Set a fixed foreground and check the weather for a sustained clear interval.
Focus manually and test one 20 s frame for sky clipping.
Set the shortest practical interval gap with sufficient battery and storage.
Capture at least 30 minutes without moving the rig.
Lighten-stack the series and inspect gaps, aircraft and passing lights.

essential: Interval timer or repeated timed capture

problems.cause: Long gaps between exposures
problems.fix: Shorten overhead and disable in-camera long-exposure dark frames.

problems.cause: Tripod movement
problems.fix: Use solid ground and avoid touching the rig.

problems.cause: Individual frames too bright
problems.fix: Lower ISO or shorten each frame while maintaining total sequence duration.

problems.cause: Dew or focus drift
problems.fix: Protect against condensation and refocus between complete sequences.

alternatives.name: Moonlit foreground
alternatives.effect: Holds a bright moonlit landscape and darker sky frames.
alternatives.requirements: Moonlight or bright ambient sky; test highlights.

alternatives.name: More faint-star trails
alternatives.effect: Reveals more stars but brightens the background.
alternatives.requirements: Dark sky and a lens with acceptable wide-open corners.

tip: Take a clean foreground frame before the sequence in case passing lights later spoil the ground.
startingPoint: Judge exposure from one frame and trail length from the total planned sequence.

title: Full Moon detail
conditions: A clear uneclipsed full Moon reasonably high above the horizon and away from severe heat shimmer.
intent: A crisp lunar disc with dark maria and bright terrain below clipping.

setup.focusTarget: Focus with a small AF point on the lunar rim, then magnify and refine manually if needed.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: The Moon is sunlit. Begin at low ISO and a fast shutter; haze may require more ISO or 1/125 s. Inspect the bright surface, not the black sky.

phone.mode: Normal photo or supported manual telephoto mode
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap and lock on the Moon.
phone.focal: Optical telephoto camera if fitted; avoid heavy digital zoom.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Use a genuine optical telephoto camera and reduce exposure until the disc shows detail.
phone.limitation: The Moon stays small without optical reach; computational lunar enhancement is not captured optical detail.
why: The full Moon is sunlit, so a brightened night-sky exposure usually turns it into a featureless white circle.
Genuine optical reach helps lunar detail; very large digital zoom cannot create optical information that the lens did not record.
Firm support and a short capture reduce shake at high magnification. The phone's fixed aperture leaves exposure adjustment or supported shutter/ISO controls to manage brightness.
steps: Choose a clear view with the Moon reasonably high, avoiding hot roofs that distort the image.
Support the phone and select a real optical telephoto camera if fitted; otherwise keep a wider view and accept a small lunar disc.
Use normal photo mode first, tap the lunar rim and lock focus/exposure if the app supports it.
Lower exposure until the bright disc shows visible tonal differences; disable night capture if it is washing out the Moon.
Use the timer and take several short captures, then enlarge the lunar edge and compare detail between frames.
If using a manual app, try its supported short shutter and low ISO controls; verify the physical telephoto camera remains selected and check the actual result.

essential: Phone; optical telephoto is needed for substantial direct lunar detail

problems.cause: Automatic exposure followed the dark sky or used a long night capture
problems.fix: Tap the Moon, reduce exposure and compare normal mode with night mode disabled where possible.

problems.cause: Heavy digital enlargement or scene-specific enhancement
problems.fix: Use a genuine optical setting and retain the original file; do not describe algorithmically reconstructed detail as an optical capture.

problems.symptom: The edge doubles in some frames
problems.cause: Phone movement during capture
problems.fix: Secure the support, use the timer and avoid touching the screen during exposure.

problems.cause: Insufficient optical focal length
problems.fix: Choose a wider landscape composition instead of forcing extreme digital zoom; a properly aligned telescope adapter is a separate equipment route.

phone.tip: Compare several modest optical-zoom frames before selecting the most enlarged one; apparent size is not the same as recorded detail.
phone.intent: A clearly bounded, correctly exposed full Moon, with surface detail where the optics resolve it; otherwise keep the small disc in a wider sky composition.

why: The bright sunlit surface needs much less exposure than its black surroundings imply.
A fast shutter limits vibration and lunar drift at high magnification.
A higher Moon usually suffers less atmospheric disturbance than one near the horizon.
steps: Choose clear air and avoid looking over a hot roof.
Secure the long lens and leave margin around the lunar disc.
Focus on the rim and use a timer or remote.
Take a short series at 1/250 s.
Inspect terrain and edges enlarged; shorten exposure for clipping and compare frames for atmospheric steadiness.

essential: Long lens or suitable telescope adapter

problems.cause: Exposure followed the black sky
problems.fix: Reduce ISO or shorten shutter in manual mode.

problems.cause: Atmospheric seeing
problems.fix: Wait for steadier air and take several frames.

problems.cause: Camera or shutter vibration
problems.fix: Use delayed/remote release and a suitable shutter mode.

problems.cause: Insufficient optical reach
problems.fix: Use a longer lens or make an environmental composition.

alternatives.name: Handheld stabilised telephoto
alternatives.effect: A faster shutter and stabilisation reduce vibration at comparable brightness.
alternatives.requirements: Effective stabilisation and steady technique.

alternatives.name: Short detail sequence
alternatives.effect: More chances of catching momentarily steady atmosphere.
alternatives.requirements: Burst/stacking workflow with unclipped frames.

tip: Full-Moon illumination is nearly frontal, so crater shadows look flatter than at quarter phase.
startingPoint: Test the lunar surface and adjust for haze and lens transmission; empty sky should remain dark.

title: Crescent and quarter Moon
conditions: A crescent or quarter Moon with sunlight skimming crater walls near the terminator.
intent: Strong crater relief along the lunar day-night boundary.

setup.focusTarget: Magnify a lit crater wall near the terminator and focus for the smallest crisp ridge. Check a recorded frame.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Adjust ISO for the lit terrain. Thin crescents or low altitude may need more exposure; raise ISO before allowing a very slow shutter at long focal length.

phone.mode: Normal photo with optical telephoto
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Auto; shorten if the crescent clips
phone.focus: Lock on the bright crescent edge.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Reduce brightness enough to define the phase and steady the phone.
phone.limitation: Most phones show the phase more readily than fine crater relief.
why: The illuminated edge needs far less exposure than the black sky, so automatic night brightening can erase the phase.
Crater shadows near the terminator need optical resolution and steady support; the phone's zoom slider alone does not provide either.
Normal capture preserves the lit crescent more reliably than a long stack aimed at revealing the dark surroundings.
steps: Check the local phase, altitude and clear-sky window; choose a viewpoint away from heat rising off roofs.
Support the phone and select genuine optical telephoto if available, keeping the entire lunar shape inside the frame.
In normal photo mode, tap the illuminated lunar edge and lock focus if supported.
Reduce exposure until the crescent or quarter-phase boundary is defined; make several timer-triggered captures.
Enlarge the recorded terminator. If detail is unstable, compare frames; if the whole crescent is white, reduce exposure further.
If optical reach is insufficient, make a clean phase silhouette against twilight instead of expecting tiny crater detail from digital zoom.

essential: Clear view of the illuminated Moon

problems.symptom: The crescent looks thicker than expected
problems.cause: Clipping and glare obscure its true boundary
problems.fix: Lower exposure, clean the lens and compare a short normal capture with night mode disabled.

problems.symptom: No craters appear at maximum zoom
problems.cause: The optical image is too small or strongly processed
problems.fix: Return to the clearest genuine optical setting and emphasise phase shape; use suitable telescope equipment for substantially more detail.

problems.cause: The small Moon gives autofocus too little contrast
problems.fix: Lock focus on the bright limb, or use magnified manual focus in an app that supports the chosen camera.

problems.cause: The exposure deliberately preserves the sunlit terrain
problems.fix: Use the earthshine sheet for the faint hemisphere; it requires a different brightness compromise.

phone.tip: A sharp, correctly exposed crescent shape is a successful phone result even when the lens cannot resolve individual craters.
phone.intent: A sharply defined crescent or quarter-phase outline, with fine crater relief only where the optical view genuinely resolves it.

why: Low-angle sunlight makes crater relief more visible than full-Moon lighting.
A moderate aperture avoids unnecessary diffraction.
Exposing for sunlit terrain deliberately leaves the unlit hemisphere dark.
steps: Check the phase and local altitude.
Frame the terminator with margin for lunar movement.
Focus on a magnified lit crater rim.
Take several 1/125 s test frames.
Inspect shadow boundaries for focus, vibration and clipping before changing ISO.

problems.cause: Too much exposure
problems.fix: Lower ISO or shorten shutter.

problems.cause: Exposure favours sunlit terrain
problems.fix: Use the earthshine sheet if the faint side is the goal.

problems.cause: Atmospheric turbulence
problems.fix: Take a sequence and choose the sharpest frame.

problems.cause: Support or shutter vibration
problems.fix: Use delayed release and stiffen support.

alternatives.name: Thin crescent
alternatives.effect: More light for a fainter low crescent.
alternatives.requirements: Clear horizon and careful focus through haze.

alternatives.name: Brighter quarter, faster shutter
alternatives.effect: Less movement sensitivity at similar brightness.
alternatives.requirements: Enough ISO quality for the required detail.

tip: The terminator moves each day, changing which craters have useful shadow relief.
startingPoint: Judge the first exposure from the illuminated terrain, not from the black surrounding sky.

title: Moon in a landscape
conditions: A rising or setting Moon during twilight, with enough remaining light to record the landscape.
intent: A naturally scaled Moon aligned with a distant ridge, tree or building.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a genuinely distant landmark and check the Moon too. If both cannot be sharp, stop down or choose a more distant foreground.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start by retaining detail in the sunlit lunar disc. Twilight narrows the brightness gap but may still leave the land dark. If needed, make a separate longer exposure for the foreground at the same framing and focal length, and disclose the blend. Increase lunar exposure only if actual haze dims the disc; inspect its highlights.

phone.mode: Normal photo with exposure lock
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Auto; avoid long lunar night stacks
phone.focus: Focus on the distant skyline.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Use optical telephoto while the sky still has colour and lower exposure enough to retain lunar shape.
phone.limitation: A single phone frame may not hold both lunar terrain and a dark foreground.
why: Twilight gives the landscape a better chance of sharing one exposure with the much brighter lunar disc.
A distant landmark can sit near the Moon's focus distance; a very close foreground may remain soft when the Moon is sharp.
Moving farther from the landmark and using genuine optical telephoto changes its scale relative to the Moon; digital enlargement alone enlarges both.
steps: Plan the Moon's altitude and direction for the exact place and date, including the real terrain horizon.
Choose a safe distant landmark before twilight and decide whether the main camera or optical telephoto gives the better relationship.
Steady the phone, tap the distant landmark or lunar edge and check that both are acceptably sharp.
Use normal photo mode and lower exposure enough to retain the lunar shape while checking the landscape.
If the landscape becomes black, accept a silhouette or make a separate brighter land frame at identical framing for a disclosed blend.
Retake as the alignment changes; enlarge the Moon to check that night processing or digital zoom has not replaced detail with a bright smear.

essential: Phone and a safe planned viewpoint

problems.symptom: The Moon is a white spot above a bright landscape
problems.cause: Automatic exposure or HDR favoured the ground
problems.fix: Lower exposure for the Moon; accept darker land or capture separate exposures for a clearly disclosed blend.

problems.symptom: The Moon looks small beside the landmark
problems.cause: The camera is too close to the landmark for the intended scale
problems.fix: Move farther away where safe and use genuine optical telephoto to restore the landmark's framing.

problems.symptom: Landmark is sharp but the Moon is soft
problems.cause: The landmark is too near or lunar detail is beyond the phone's optics
problems.fix: Choose a more distant landmark, refocus and inspect a recorded frame; avoid relying on digital zoom to repair it.

problems.symptom: The Moon has a doubled edge after a night capture
problems.cause: Motion or failed computational alignment
problems.fix: Use firm support and compare a shorter normal exposure while twilight still illuminates the land.

phone.tip: Frame a small bright Moon deliberately if necessary; a convincing alignment is more valuable than an oversized processed disc.

why: Twilight brings foreground brightness closer to the sunlit Moon.
Moving farther from the foreground allows a longer lens to make the Moon larger relative to it.
A short shutter preserves the lunar edge at telephoto magnification.
steps: Plan Moon altitude and azimuth for the exact location, date and real terrain horizon.
Choose a distant foreground and safe position before twilight.
Focus and verify both landmark and Moon.
Test exposure for the lunar disc.
If the foreground is too dark, make a separate longer foreground exposure from the same framing for a disclosed blend; keep the short lunar frame.
Watch the alignment change and reframe before the Moon touches an unwanted edge.

problems.symptom: Moon too small beside the landmark
problems.cause: Viewpoint too close to the landmark
problems.fix: Move farther away and use a longer lens to restore landmark framing.

problems.cause: Scene exceeds one-frame dynamic range
problems.fix: Work earlier in twilight or bracket for a disclosed blend.

problems.cause: Focus-distance mismatch or lunar motion
problems.fix: Check both focus distances and shorten shutter.

problems.cause: Wrong viewpoint or idealised horizon assumption
problems.fix: Check actual terrain and adjust position in advance.

alternatives.effect: A smaller Moon in a broader twilight landscape; this brighter exposure favours the land and may clip lunar surface detail.
alternatives.requirements: Around 35–50 mm equivalent. Accept a small bright disc, or retain a separate short lunar exposure for a disclosed blend.

alternatives.name: Foreground silhouette
alternatives.effect: A clear dark outline beneath a detailed Moon.
alternatives.requirements: Recognisable foreground shape and suitable alignment.

tip: For a plausible blend, keep viewpoint, focal length and the Moon’s original scale unchanged.

title: Aurora curtains
conditions: Visible auroral curtains under clear dark skies, changing shape within seconds.
intent: Distinct rays and folds above a grounded foreground rather than a smooth green wash.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a magnified star, verify a test image and leave focus fixed while the display moves.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Fast curtains need 0.5–2 s and more ISO. A faint slow arc may need 5–8 s; watch for smeared rays and green-channel clipping.

phone.mode: Night mode; manual app for fast rays
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Lock distant focus.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Brace the main camera and shorten the night capture if the display moves rapidly.
phone.limitation: Long computational stacks may erase curtain structure even when they look brighter.
why: Auroral curtains can change faster than stars move, so a long phone night capture may brighten the sky while erasing its shape.
The main camera and firm support give the phone the best chance to separate a faint arc from noise.
The aperture is usually fixed; the available capture duration and exposure adjustment are the practical controls unless a manual app exposes shutter and ISO.

title: Meteor shower
conditions: A meteor-shower period with clear dark skies and the radiant above the local horizon.
intent: A meteor streak across recognisable stars, found in a long repeating capture sequence.

setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Repeat 8 s frames with minimal gaps. A faster lens or more ISO helps a faint meteor; extending time mainly brightens the sky because each meteor is brief.

setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.

phone.mode: Normal photo first; short night mode if needed

phone.focus: Tap and lock a distant horizon edge.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.

why: These clouds remain sunlit in twilight, so normal photo mode may retain more fine ripples than a long night stack.

steps: Check local summer visibility and the twilight horizon for your latitude and hemisphere; do not assume every bright night cloud is noctilucent.
Support the main camera and frame the strongest silver-blue ripples above a narrow dark horizon.
Tap a distant high-contrast skyline edge and lock focus if available.

title: Lunar eclipse totality
conditions: The Moon is within Earth’s umbra, with brightness ranging from orange-red to very dark brown.
intent: A detailed coloured eclipsed Moon with controlled lunar-motion blur.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a bright lunar edge before totality, then lock manually and check an enlarged recorded frame during the dark phase.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Totality brightness varies widely. Start at 0.5 s and bracket one or two stops. Open aperture or raise ISO before extending beyond a sharp motion limit.

phone.mode: Optical telephoto with supported manual/night mode
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Shortest useful capture for the dark disc
phone.focus: Lock lunar focus before totality.
phone.focal: Optical telephoto for disc; main camera for landscape.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Brace the phone and expose for the coloured Moon; a wider landscape may work better than heavy digital zoom.
phone.limitation: Small optics and long computational stacks may fail to preserve lunar detail.
why: The eclipsed Moon can become many stops dimmer than the preceding bright disc, so one locked exposure cannot cover the entire event.
Optical telephoto helps scale but may perform poorly in deep totality; the main camera can give a better wider landscape result.
A long phone stack can blur or reshape the moving lunar edge even on a tripod, so examine recorded detail rather than choosing only the brightest preview.
steps: Check local eclipse contact times, Moon altitude and weather, then choose a safe clear view.
Clamp the phone and test its genuine optical telephoto while the Moon is still bright; keep a wider main-camera composition as a fallback.
Lock focus on the lunar rim before totality if the app permits, and record a test to confirm focus rather than assuming the lock is correct.
As totality begins, compare available normal and short night captures; adjust brightness for the coloured disc without changing framing unnecessarily.
Enlarge the recorded rim and surface. If long captures smear detail, shorten the supported capture or use a wider view; manual shutter/ISO changes require a compatible app.
Reduce exposure promptly when a bright sunlit limb returns; a lunar eclipse itself needs no solar filter.

essential: Local eclipse times and a clear horizon

problems.symptom: The red Moon is nearly invisible
problems.cause: Totality is dark and the phone's telephoto camera has limited light collection
problems.fix: Increase available exposure cautiously, compare the main camera's wider view, and accept a small coloured disc if fine detail is beyond the optics.

problems.symptom: The Moon brightens but its edge becomes soft or doubled

problems.fix: Use a shorter supported capture and firmer support; a brighter result is not useful if it loses the disc's shape.

problems.symptom: Focus hunts during the darkest phase
problems.cause: The faint lunar edge has insufficient contrast
problems.fix: Use the earlier verified focus lock, or manual focus in an app that supports the selected camera; avoid repeated unsuccessful tapping.

problems.symptom: The returning bright limb is blown white
problems.cause: The phone retained totality's brightened exposure

Higher ISO and a wider aperture preserve a motion-limiting shutter at long focal length.
Fixed Daylight colour gives a consistent starting point for the changing lunar colour.
steps: Check contact times and local horizon visibility.
Set up and focus during the bright partial phase.
At totality, test the listed exposure and bracket.
Enlarge rim and crater detail to separate motion from noise.
Use higher ISO for a shorter time or a tracker for substantially longer exposures.
Return to short exposures as direct sunlight reappears.

problems.fix: Shorten shutter or use a tracking mount.

title: Partial solar eclipse — filtered
conditions: A partial or annular eclipse imaged only through an intact purpose-made solar filter secured over the front of the lens.
intent: A sharply defined filtered solar crescent with retained surface detail where optics and atmosphere permit.

setup.focusTarget: With the correct front solar filter secured first, use magnified electronic live view to focus on the solar limb. Never use an unfiltered optical viewfinder.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: This is a trial only: solar-filter transmission differs. Follow the filter maker’s guidance, bracket and adjust shutter for unclipped detail while leaving the filter fitted.

phone.mode: Properly filtered capture; otherwise photograph projected crescents
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Auto with exposure reduction behind safe filtration
phone.focus: Focus on the filtered disc or projection surface.
phone.focal: Optical telephoto only behind correct solar filtration.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Use a securely fitted purpose-made filter appropriate to the device, or point away from the Sun and photograph pinhole projections.
phone.limitation: A phone is not exempt from solar hazards. Eclipse glasses, sunglasses and photographic ND are not substitutes for an appropriate camera solar filter.
why: A rear screen does not protect the camera optics from direct sunlight; direct eclipse imaging still requires appropriate secure front filtration.
A pinhole projection lets the phone photograph a crescent on a surface while facing away from the Sun, providing a practical alternative to direct imaging.
For filtered imaging, filter transmission and automatic camera switching affect the result; exposure adjustment never substitutes for safe filtration.
steps: Choose the route before aiming: photograph pinhole projections with the Sun behind you, or obtain a purpose-made solar filter suitable for the phone and follow its maker's instructions.
For projection, point the phone at the projected crescents on a shaded surface; never look toward the Sun through the projector's opening.

For direct imaging, inspect and secure the appropriate filter over every active lens before pointing sunward; prevent automatic switching to an uncovered camera and stop if protection cannot be assured.
Support the phone. Tap the projection surface, or focus the safely filtered solar limb using the screen; use supported focus lock if available.
Take a brief test and lower exposure if the crescent is featureless. Keep the phone's aperture automatic/fixed; use only the exposure controls the app actually offers.
Keep filtration secured throughout all partial and annular phases. If it loosens or is damaged, stop and point away from the Sun before handling it; this sheet does not cover unfiltered totality.

essential: For projection: a pinhole projector and suitable surface; for direct imaging: an intact purpose-made solar filter securely fitted to the active optics
optional: Spare inspected solar filter for the direct route
Separate certified solar viewer for unaided viewing, never as protection behind camera optics

Secure it over the front objective before aiming at the Sun; protect any separate finder too.
Frame using electronic live view with filtration already in place.

title: Earthshine on a crescent Moon
conditions: A thin young or old crescent in twilight, with faint Earth-reflected light illuminating its unlit hemisphere.

title: Sunrise reflected in water
conditions: A calm shoreline just before or after sunrise, with coloured sky reflected in gentle ripples.

title: Golden-hour dune ridges
conditions: Low side light crossing sand ridges, with crisp shadow boundaries and no strong blowing sand.
intent: Sculpted dune shapes with warm highlights, cool shadows and minimal clutter.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on the main ridge line; check both near ripples and distant ridges if they are included.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Keep the sunlit sand below clipping while allowing shadows to remain deep. Change shutter for light level; use f/11 if multiple nearby ridges need extra depth.

phone.mode: Normal photo with optical telephoto if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap the ridge where light meets shadow.
phone.focal: Optical telephoto or main lens; no heavy digital zoom.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Frame a small set of curves and let shadows stay dark; avoid walking into the intended foreground.

why: Low side light shapes a dune through alternating bright and dark ridges; lifting every shadow flattens that structure.

A phone's fixed aperture does not provide a depth slider for the sand; camera position and avoiding an excessively close foreground determine how much is sharp.
steps: Plan a safe route with appropriate water and sun protection, and keep footprints out of the sand you intend to photograph.
Find sunlight crossing the dunes from the side and select two or three clear intersecting curves.
Choose the main camera for near ripples or genuine optical telephoto for distant ridges; avoid heavy digital zoom.
Tap the main light-shadow boundary to focus and make a normal-mode test.
Inspect bright sand texture and the nearest important ridge; lower exposure for clipping and move back if the foreground is outside the sharp zone.
Reframe as the shadow line changes, preserving its depth instead of forcing HDR to brighten every dark area.

essential: Water and sun protection appropriate to the route

title: Mountain vista
conditions: Clear daylight or broken cloud over distant peaks, with a stable foreground and moderate wind.
intent: A readable mountain landscape with a deliberate foreground and sharp distant detail.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a distinct mid-distance ridge or foreground feature, then enlarge both the nearest important object and the far peaks.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Begin at f/8. If near and far detail cannot both resolve, use f/11 or move the near foreground farther away; raise ISO if wind demands a faster shutter.

phone.mode: Normal photo with HDR when needed
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap a mid-distance high-contrast ridge.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Keep the horizon level and choose one foreground route or shape leading toward the main peak.
phone.limitation: Very wide views make mountains look small; the main or optical telephoto camera may suit the scene better than ultrawide.
why: The phone's ultrawide camera can make an impressive mountain look small by including too much foreground and sky.
One clear foreground line establishes scale, but placing it extremely close can exceed the phone's usable depth of field.
HDR can balance clouds and shaded land, although moving foliage or strong processing may create unnatural edges.
steps: Choose a safe viewpoint and identify the one peak or ridge that should dominate the photograph.
Compare the main camera with genuine optical telephoto before choosing ultrawide; include only a useful foreground line.
Level the phone and tap a distinct mid-distance feature or ridge to focus.
Take a normal test and check bright cloud texture, then compare restrained HDR if the shaded land is too dark.
Enlarge the nearest important object and the far peaks separately; move back from the foreground or refocus if both do not hold detail.
Brace against wind and retake, distinguishing atmospheric haze in distant peaks from movement affecting the whole frame.

essential: Phone and suitable equipment for the chosen safe route

problems.cause: An ultrawide view includes too much empty foreground
problems.fix: Use the main camera or genuine optical telephoto and simplify the lower part of the composition.

problems.symptom: The close foreground is sharp but peaks are not

problems.fix: Move back from the foreground, tap a farther feature and inspect both distances in another test.

problems.symptom: The whole view has slight double edges
problems.cause: Wind or hand movement during capture
problems.fix: Brace the phone safely, use normal capture in adequate light or support it for a longer capture.

problems.symptom: Clouds are blank white above a detailed valley
problems.cause: Automatic exposure favoured the shaded land
problems.fix: Lower exposure or compare restrained HDR, checking cloud texture and avoiding halos along the skyline.

phone.tip: Compare a main-camera frame with the ultrawide version before leaving; the tighter view often communicates the mountain's scale better.

why: f/8 provides useful depth without automatically choosing the smallest aperture.
Foreground placement establishes scale and direction toward the peak.
A reasonably fast shutter resists wind vibration when handheld.
steps: Find a clear view and decide which peak is the main subject.
Choose a foreground line without letting it cover the mountain base.
Focus and take the starting frame.
Enlarge near and far detail and check bright cloud texture.
Change focus/aperture for depth, or shutter/ISO for brightness and wind.

title: Layered ridges in haze
conditions: Distant ridges separated by haze in soft morning or evening light.
intent: Overlapping silhouettes that become lighter and lower in contrast with distance.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a well-defined ridge in the layered group; distant ridges are generally close together in focus distance at this scale.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Keep a fast enough shutter for the long lens. Adjust ISO rather than risking handheld blur; avoid forcing the brightest haze into clipped white.

phone.mode: Normal photo with optical telephoto
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap a clear dark ridge.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Use a tighter view of several repeating ridges; leave the natural fading contrast intact.
phone.limitation: Heavy digital zoom and aggressive dehaze can make layers look artificial.
why: Each successive ridge loses contrast through the atmosphere; preserving that difference is what creates depth.
A genuine optical telephoto view isolates the repeating shapes without relying on large digital enlargement.
A small hand movement is more visible in a tight view, so support can improve ridge edges without trying to remove natural haze.
steps: Find a safe view across several overlapping ridges with a clear light-to-dark progression.
Choose genuine optical telephoto if available; otherwise compose a simpler main-camera frame and crop only modestly.
Brace the phone and tap a distinct darker ridge edge to focus.
Take a normal test, adjusting brightness so the lightest haze retains tone rather than clipping to white.
Enlarge the nearest visible ridge to check shake, then judge the softer distant layers as atmosphere rather than automatically refocusing.
Keep a restrained edit and leave space above the lightest ridge so the progression remains readable.

essential: Phone and a safe clear viewpoint
optional: Small support for dim first light

problems.symptom: Every ridge becomes equally dark and crisp
problems.cause: Excessive dehaze or contrast removes atmospheric separation
problems.fix: Reduce processing and preserve the natural lightening of distant layers.

phone.tip: Use the nearest ridge to judge technical sharpness and the farthest ridge to judge atmosphere; they should not necessarily look equally crisp.

why: A telephoto view isolates the repeating shapes from distracting foreground.

Long focal length makes a firm support or faster shutter valuable.
steps: Look across successive ridges rather than directly at one isolated peak.
Choose a frame with clear overlap and a rhythm of light-to-dark layers.
Focus on an edge with reliable contrast.
Test the starting exposure and inspect the nearest visible ridge for sharpness.
Adjust shutter/ISO for shake and brightness while preserving the haze.

problems.fix: Change viewpoint or time of day and shield stray light.

problems.fix: Use a faster shutter or support.

problems.fix: Reduce local contrast and preserve atmospheric fading.

title: Forest interior and canopy
conditions: A shaded forest with fairly still leaves, soft overcast light or a limited patch of filtered sunlight.
intent: Ordered tree shapes and rich foliage without distracting blown-out sky gaps.

setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Use 1/30 s only when leaves are still. For wind, move toward 1/125–1/250 s and raise ISO; keep bright sky gaps from setting an impossible exposure.

phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap the main trunk.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.

why: A few organised trunks give a phone forest photograph structure; extra ultrawide coverage can add more clutter than interest.
Tree bark may remain sharp during a supported night capture while moving leaves blur or ghost between frames.
Avoiding bright sky gaps reduces the brightness range the phone must process and keeps attention on the woodland.
steps: Find a path, main trunk or small group of trees with clear spacing, staying on safe permitted ground.
Use the main camera and move sideways to remove bright sky holes and overlapping branches at the edges.
Tap the trunk anchoring the composition and take a braced normal-mode test.
Enlarge bark and leaf edges separately. If the woodland is still but too dark, compare a supported night capture.
If leaves move, prefer normal capture, wait for a lull or choose a brighter patch; a tripod will not freeze the foliage.
Adjust exposure to retain sunlit leaves and compare restrained HDR only if it avoids moving-leaf artifacts.

optional: Phone tripod for still dim scenes

Focus on the anchor trunk and use a timer for the first frame.

Raise shutter/ISO for wind, or bracket a still scene if contrast remains high.

title: Near foreground to distant horizon
conditions: A still landscape with a near rock or flower patch and a distant horizon, viewed with a wide lens.

setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.

title: Fog and isolated trees

setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Do not force bright snow to the meter’s zero. Lengthen shutter or raise ISO until snow looks bright but its sunlit texture is not clipped.

phone.mode: Normal photo with HDR if needed
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap a dark edge at the desired distance.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Raise exposure a little if snow looks grey, then check that bright ridges still have detail.
phone.limitation: The screen’s outdoor brightness can mislead; inspect the image rather than relying on display brilliance.
why: A snow-filled frame can fool automatic exposure into making white snow grey; small exposure adjustments matter more than a phone aperture setting.
Side light and shadows reveal snow texture, while a dark tree or rock gives shape to an otherwise blank scene.
Blue snow shadows can be natural sky light; neutralising every blue area may make the scene less believable.
steps: Choose safe ground and look for light raking across snow, with a tree, rock or shadow as a composition anchor.
Use the main camera and tap a defined edge at the important distance; avoid trying to focus on featureless white snow.
Take a normal-mode test and raise exposure a little if snow looks grey.
Inspect the brightest sunlit ridges for texture; lower exposure again if they clip and compare restrained HDR for deep shaded areas.
Enlarge the anchor to check focus and keep natural blue shade unless it is clearly an unwanted colour cast.
Keep the phone within its manufacturer's operating temperatures and protect cold equipment from condensation during warming.

essential: Phone and suitable clothing/traction for the location

problems.fix: Tap a rock, twig or textured snow edge at the same useful distance.

problems.symptom: The image turns hazy after coming indoors
problems.cause: Condensation formed on cold equipment
problems.fix: Let the phone acclimatise without charging or using wet connectors; for future transitions seal it dry before entering warmth and follow the maker's care guidance.

phone.tip: Judge the saved snow texture in shade if possible; an automatically brightened outdoor screen can hide an exposure mistake.

why: Snow occupies the bright end of the tonal range and can fool an averaging meter into underexposure.
Moderate aperture keeps the landscape readable while retaining a fast shutter.
Blue shadows can be real reflected sky colour, so they need not all be neutralised.
steps: Find light raking across snow so texture is visible.
Include a tree, rock or shadow line to give the white scene structure.
Focus on a defined edge and take the starting frame.
Check sunlit snow for clipping and shaded snow for useful detail.
Adjust exposure manually; compare Daylight and Cloudy without removing all natural blue.

problems.cause: Underexposure from averaging meter

problems.cause: Clipped highlights or flat light

problems.cause: Featureless white target

title: Desert in harsh midday light
conditions: Bright overhead sun in an arid landscape, with high contrast and possible heat shimmer.
intent: Graphic shapes, negative space and controlled bright sand instead of forced golden-hour colour.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a nearby rock, dune edge or structure; judge distant detail for heat shimmer before changing focus repeatedly.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Bright sand may need more exposure than the meter suggests, but protect sunlit texture. Change shutter for brightness; extra shutter speed cannot remove atmospheric shimmer.

phone.mode: Normal photo
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap the main rock or ridge.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Use hard shadows as graphic shapes and keep the composition simple.
phone.limitation: Heavy zoom magnifies heat haze and loses detail; moving closer safely is better than digital enlargement.
why: Hard overhead light can make strong graphic shadows even when it does not create warm, sculpted golden-hour dunes.
A nearer subject is less affected by a long path through shimmering hot air; digital zoom cannot remove that distortion.
Bright sand needs careful exposure checking because a phone may either darken it to grey or clip it while lifting black shadows.
steps: Plan a safe short route with water and heat protection; keep the phone shaded between captures and within its operating limits.
Choose a simple nearby arrangement of sand, rock and hard shadow rather than relying on a heavily enlarged distant view.
Use normal mode on the main camera and tap the main rock or ridge edge to focus.
Take a test and inspect bright sand; adjust exposure until it is bright but still textured.
Enlarge both nearby and distant detail. If only distant edges shimmer, choose a nearer composition or cooler conditions rather than repeatedly refocusing.
Keep the deliberate shadow shapes and avoid lifting every dark area into noisy flat grey.

essential: Water and sun protection appropriate to the route

problems.symptom: Distant objects ripple or look smeared
problems.cause: Heat shimmer along the sightline
problems.fix: Use a nearer subject or return in cooler air; sharpening, digital zoom and a steadier grip do not remove atmospheric distortion.

problems.cause: Automatic exposure treated the bright sand as average tone
problems.fix: Increase exposure cautiously while checking a recorded bright patch for detail.

problems.symptom: The image has flat grey shadows and glowing edges
problems.cause: Strong HDR or local enhancement
problems.fix: Compare a restrained normal capture and let useful hard shadows remain dark.

problems.symptom: The phone dims or stops camera capture
problems.cause: Excessive operating temperature
problems.fix: Stop shooting, move the phone into shade and follow its maker's cooling guidance; do not keep it aimed in the heat to rescue the composition.

phone.tip: Look for one clean shadow shape close enough to record well; midday often rewards a simple graphic frame more than a distant panorama.

why: Harsh overhead light is suited to shape and contrast more than subtle modelling.
Low ISO preserves highlight headroom in abundant light.
A normal lens avoids exaggerating distant heat shimmer as much as a long telephoto.
steps: Plan a safe short route with water and protection from heat.
Find a simple arrangement of rock, shadow and sand.
Focus on the main solid edge and take a test.
Check bright sand texture and assess whether distant blur is atmospheric.
Adjust exposure or choose a nearer composition rather than chasing sharpness through heat haze.

essential: Water and sun protection appropriate to the location

problems.cause: Heat shimmer
problems.fix: Use a nearer subject or return during cooler conditions.

problems.cause: Meter underexposure
problems.fix: Increase exposure while protecting highlights.

problems.cause: Composition lacks graphic structure
problems.fix: Reframe around a clear shadow shape instead of lifting everything.

problems.cause: Sand on the optics or sensor
problems.fix: Protect equipment and change lenses only in sheltered conditions.

alternatives.name: Wide environmental scene

alternatives.requirements: Avoid very close foreground if depth remains insufficient.

tip: Work with the hard shadow direction. Midday can suit a graphic image even when it cannot provide warm sculpted light.

title: Beach ripples and tidal patterns
conditions: Exposed sand or shallow tidal channels with side light and relatively little water movement.
intent: Repeating patterns that lead through the frame, with edge-to-edge texture.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a clear ripple ridge near the centre of the pattern area; keep the camera roughly parallel when photographing a flat patch.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Keep f/8 for a flat pattern; use f/11 for a low oblique angle with more depth. Adjust shutter/ISO for available light and keep wet highlights under control.

phone.mode: Normal photo; avoid portrait mode
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap the main ripple ridge.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Use the grid to align a pattern or deliberately place it diagonally; keep your own shadow out.
phone.limitation: Automatic macro switching can alter perspective when too close; check the final frame.
why: Side light makes small sand ridges visible through their shadows, so camera angle and timing create the texture.
Keeping the phone roughly parallel to a flat pattern reduces the near-to-far focus problem without requiring aperture control.
Normal mode preserves repeated edges; portrait blur and unexpected macro switching can distort a pattern that should remain continuous.
steps: Check the tide and return route, then choose exposed sand or shallow channels on safe accessible ground.
Find a repeating ripple pattern and keep your footprints and shadow outside it.
Use normal main-camera capture, holding the phone roughly parallel for a flat patch or deliberately oblique for leading lines.
Tap a clear ripple ridge and take a test without moving closer than the selected lens can focus.
Inspect both ends of the pattern for sharpness and wet patches for clipping; change camera angle before resorting to artificial sharpening.
Refine the crop around one shell, broken ripple or channel while continuing to watch incoming water.

essential: Phone and knowledge of the local tide/access conditions

problems.cause: The light is too frontal or diffuse to reveal relief
problems.fix: Change direction for side light or choose a stronger physical pattern.

problems.symptom: One end of the pattern is soft
problems.cause: An oblique view exceeds the usable focus depth
problems.fix: Hold the phone more parallel to the sand, move back and refocus on the important area.

problems.symptom: The view changes suddenly when you move closer
problems.cause: Automatic macro switching selected another lens
problems.fix: Move back within the main camera's focusing range or lock the intended camera if available, then recheck framing.

problems.symptom: Your shadow or a white wet glare interrupts the pattern
problems.cause: The viewing angle blocks light or catches a specular reflection
problems.fix: Move sideways, change height or reduce exposure for glare while staying clear of incoming water.

phone.tip: One small shell or broken ripple can give a repeated pattern a focal point without adding another subject.

why: Side light defines tiny sand relief through small shadows.
Keeping the sensor plane parallel to the pattern reduces unnecessary depth-of-field demand.
A normal lens simplifies shapes without excessive wide-angle distortion.
steps: Check the tide and choose a safe exposed area.
Find a repeated rhythm with one deliberate interruption or leading channel.
Keep footprints and your shadow outside the frame.
Focus on a ridge and test the exposure.
Inspect near and far pattern edges; change camera angle or aperture if one end is soft.

optional: Polariser for selective wet glare control

problems.cause: Light is frontal or overcast
problems.fix: Use lower side light or search for stronger physical relief.

problems.symptom: Near edge sharp, far edge soft
problems.cause: Oblique angle creates depth demand
problems.fix: Raise the camera toward a parallel view or stop down.

problems.cause: Shooting angle blocks the light
problems.fix: Change position or use a longer focal length.

problems.cause: Specular reflections clip
problems.fix: Change angle, reduce exposure or rotate a polariser selectively.

alternatives.requirements: Careful near/far focus check.

title: Mirror reflection in a lake
conditions: Calm water reflecting a distant treeline or mountain, ideally sheltered from wind.
intent: A clean mirror image with deliberate symmetry and crisp reflected detail.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on the distant reflected treeline or the real treeline; a reflection is optically at the reflected subject’s apparent distance, not the nearby water surface.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Use a relatively short exposure while the water is still to retain fine reflection detail. Lengthening cannot recreate a mirror when wind breaks the reflection.

phone.mode: Normal photo
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap a clear reflected distant feature.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Level the horizon and try a centred horizon if the symmetry is the point.
phone.limitation: A polariser attachment may remove the reflection you want; compare before using it.
why: Calm water creates the mirror; a phone's long-exposure effect can blur ripples but cannot reconstruct a reflection broken by wind.
A distant reflected mountain is focused at its apparent reflected distance, not at the nearby water surface.
Normal capture holds fine reflected detail, while deliberate level framing makes the symmetry convincing.
steps: Choose a safe sheltered lakeside viewpoint and wait for a lull that gives recognisable reflected shapes.
Use the main camera, level the horizon and test a centred composition if symmetry is the point.
Tap the real distant treeline or a clear reflected distant feature to focus, avoiding nearby floating debris.
Take a normal-mode test and inspect the reflection separately from the real mountain or trees.
Adjust exposure for bright sky and reflection; compare restrained HDR only if it does not ghost the water.
Change camera height or move laterally to remove shore clutter, and remove any polarising attachment that suppresses the desired reflection.

essential: Phone and a safe calm-water viewpoint

problems.symptom: The reflection is weak or missing
problems.cause: Wind, viewing angle or polarisation
problems.fix: Wait for calm, adjust camera height and remove or rotate a polarising attachment if fitted.

problems.symptom: Floating leaves are sharp but the reflected mountain is soft
problems.cause: Focus landed on nearby debris
problems.fix: Tap the reflected distant feature or the real treeline and check another recorded frame.

problems.symptom: Reflected edges are doubled or broken
problems.cause: Water moved while HDR/night frames were combined
problems.fix: Compare a normal single-capture route and wait for calmer water rather than extending the night countdown.

problems.symptom: The mirror effect feels unbalanced despite sharp detail
problems.cause: The horizon tilts or clutter cuts the reflected subject
problems.fix: Use the level/grid and shift the viewpoint to clean up the shoreline before exposing again.

phone.tip: Tap an identifiable reflected tree or mountain edge rather than an arbitrary patch of water; the optical focus distance matters.

why: A calm surface, rather than a very long exposure, creates a true mirror.
A moderate aperture keeps shore and reflected distant detail readable.
Deliberate central symmetry can be stronger than forcing a rule-of-thirds layout.
steps: Find sheltered water and wait for a lull in wind.
Choose a clean shoreline with few branches cutting the reflected image.
Level the camera and focus on reflected distant detail.
Take the starting frame and inspect the reflection separately.
Adjust height for a better reflection shape; remove a polariser if it weakens the result.

problems.cause: Wind or polarisation
problems.fix: Wait for calmer water and reduce polariser effect.

problems.cause: Camera not level
problems.fix: Use the level/grid and correct before exposing.

problems.symptom: Near ripples sharp, reflected mountain soft
problems.cause: Focus at wrong distance
problems.fix: Focus on the reflected distant feature.

problems.symptom: Clutter cuts across the mirror image
problems.cause: Low branches or floating debris in composition
problems.fix: Move laterally or tighten the frame.

alternatives.effect: An inverted abstract view without the real subject.
alternatives.requirements: Tighter framing and a recognisable reflected shape.

alternatives.name: Gentle ripple version
alternatives.effect: Softens small disturbances for a less literal reflection.
alternatives.requirements: Tripod and about three additional stops of ND in unchanged light, or light about three stops dimmer; meter again. A longer exposure does not restore a mirror in windy water.

title: Rainbow after rain
conditions: Rain or fine spray ahead of you with low sunlight behind you and a darker sky beyond.
intent: A clear coloured arc grounded in a landscape, with its brightest colours preserved.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a distant landscape edge; the rainbow itself is not a solid object to focus on.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Expose for the lit arc and clouds, then adjust shutter as sunlight changes. Rotate a polariser cautiously: some orientations can greatly weaken the rainbow.

phone.mode: Normal photo, main or ultrawide for the whole arc
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap the distant landscape.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Keep the Sun behind you, find a dark background for contrast and lower exposure if the sky clips.
phone.limitation: Strong automatic saturation can exaggerate colours; keep a natural version.
why: The Sun behind you and rain ahead create the viewing geometry; no exposure setting can keep the rainbow after that alignment disappears.
A wide or ultrawide camera can include the arc, while a main-camera view of one end can give a stronger relationship to a landmark.
A darker background makes the colours visible without excessive saturation, and clean optics prevent raindrops from scattering the light.
steps: Watch opposite the Sun as rain clears and choose a safe viewpoint; if thunder is heard, move into substantial enclosed shelter.
Use the main camera for one end and a landmark, or try ultrawide if the whole arc will not fit.
Tap a distant landscape edge to focus and take a normal test promptly before the light changes.
Lower exposure if the bright clouds clip, checking that the arc still has believable colour.
Inspect for water droplets on the lens and processing halos; clean the lens from shelter and compare a restrained capture.
Reframe around a darker background or a simpler landmark rather than forcing saturation when the rainbow weakens.

problems.symptom: The rainbow fades as you prepare the shot
problems.cause: Sunlight or rain geometry changed
problems.fix: Capture a quick normal frame first and watch for sunlight to return; a longer exposure cannot restore a vanished arc.

problems.symptom: The whole arc is cut off
problems.cause: The selected camera's field is too narrow
problems.fix: Use ultrawide if available or compose one end with a landmark; a panorama needs a stable arc and careful overlap.

problems.symptom: Soft bright blobs cover the colours
problems.cause: Raindrops or fingerprints on the lens
problems.fix: Clean the lens safely under shelter and retake before the light changes.

problems.symptom: Colours look fake or the arc nearly disappears
problems.cause: Excessive enhancement or a polariser attachment suppressing the rainbow
problems.fix: Keep a natural reference, reduce enhancement and remove or rotate any polariser while checking its effect.

phone.tip: Get one simple frame immediately, then improve the composition; a rainbow can change faster than the phone's editing controls.

why: The rainbow is most visible when sunlight behind the camera meets rain ahead.
A wide field helps fit the arc while a land anchor gives scale.
A polariser can change the rainbow’s visibility, so its effect must be watched rather than assumed.
steps: Look opposite the Sun when rain clears and light breaks through.
Find a safe viewpoint with a darker background and a simple foreground.
Frame quickly before the light changes and focus on the distant land.
Test exposure, checking the bright sky and arc colour.
Try tighter framing of one end if the whole arc lacks a strong composition.

problems.cause: Sun/rain geometry changed or polariser suppresses it
problems.fix: Remove/rotate the filter and wait for sunlight to return.

problems.symptom: Colours weak against a pale sky
problems.cause: Poor background contrast
problems.fix: Frame the arc against darker clouds or terrain.

problems.cause: Water on front element
problems.fix: Shelter and wipe the lens carefully.

problems.cause: Field of view too narrow
problems.fix: Use a wider lens or make a quick overlapping panorama if the arc is stable.

alternatives.name: Whole double arc
alternatives.effect: Includes more sky and possibly the fainter outer arc.
alternatives.requirements: Very wide lens and controlled foreground.

alternatives.name: Arc end with landmark
alternatives.effect: Stronger subject relationship and saturated local colour.
alternatives.requirements: Telephoto/normal framing and a distant landmark.

tip: A rainbow moves with your viewpoint; treat it as an alignment opportunity rather than something with a fixed physical endpoint.
startingPoint: Test quickly and keep watching the light; a technically ideal setting is useless after the arc fades.
