title: Lightning from enclosed shelter
conditions: A distant night storm photographed with a pre-positioned camera and remote release while the photographer remains inside substantial enclosed shelter.
intent: A defined lightning channel against a controlled sky without exposing the photographer to the storm.

setup.focusTarget: Before the storm reaches the location, focus on a distant light/skyline edge and lock manual focus. Do not go outside to refocus during thunder.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: A 5 s frame is a chance window for a strike, not the flash duration. Aperture and ISO mainly govern bolt brightness; shutter also accumulates ambient sky light.

phone.mode: Remote interval/manual capture only if safely supported
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Lock distant focus before the storm.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Position the device safely in advance and operate remotely while staying away from windows, doors and wired equipment.
phone.limitation: A normal handheld phone reaction is usually too slow; safety and shelter take priority over capture.
why: A remote repeating capture can include an unpredictable bolt without requiring the photographer to react at an exposed window.
The bolt is much briefer than the capture window. Shortening that window mainly reduces ambient sky brightness and may not make a clipped bolt darker.
Phone aperture is normally fixed; bolt brightness control may depend on genuinely available manual ISO or exposure controls, so the technique has device limits.
steps: Choose substantial enclosed shelter and verify a remote capture route that lets you remain away from windows, doors, plumbing and wired equipment.
Before thunder approaches, position a battery-powered phone securely, protected appropriately for its placement; do not run a mains connection to an exposed setup.
Focus on a distant skyline or light and lock it if supported, then test the remote interval/manual operation before the storm.
Remain safely sheltered and start the preconfigured repeating sequence remotely; if the phone cannot be operated this way, skip the photograph.

Review remotely if possible. Reduce available exposure or manual ISO for a clipped bolt; shorten a supported capture window for an overly bright sky, recognising that these controls may not be available.
Do not approach windows or retrieve outdoor equipment to improve framing. Follow local warnings and wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before going outside.

essential: Battery-powered phone on pre-positioned stable support
Verified wireless remote/interval capture route that does not require standing at a window
optional: Weather-appropriate phone housing installed before the storm
Compatible manual/interval app tested in advance

problems.symptom: No lightning appears in the sequence
problems.cause: Strikes missed the frame or occurred between captures
problems.fix: Use shorter supported gaps or a wider view only if this can be changed remotely while remaining sheltered; accept a missed shot otherwise.

problems.symptom: Bolts are thick white featureless lines
problems.cause: The brief flash exceeded the phone's exposure range
problems.fix: Lower genuine manual ISO or available exposure adjustment remotely if supported; shortening the overall window alone may not dim the bolt.

problems.symptom: The sky is bright even without a strike
problems.cause: The repeating capture accumulates too much ambient light
problems.fix: Shorten the supported capture window or reduce brightness remotely, keeping distant focus locked.

problems.symptom: Reflections obscure a view through glass
problems.cause: Interior lights or the phone screen reflect in the window
problems.fix: Use a preplanned remote setup with interior reflections minimised; do not move to an open window, balcony or exposed opening during the storm.

phone.tip: Test focus, framing and remote operation before storm conditions develop; if correcting the setup would expose you to lightning hazards, leave it alone.

why: The lightning flash is brief; leaving the shutter open increases the chance of including it.
Low ISO and moderate aperture reduce the chance of a featureless white bolt.
A remote setup allows the photographer to remain away from exposed positions and window frames.
steps: Identify substantial enclosed shelter and assess whether photography can be done without exposure to lightning hazards.
Before thunder approaches, position the battery-powered camera safely and pre-focus at distance.
Remain inside away from windows, doors, plumbing and wired electrical equipment; trigger remotely.
Use repeated 5 s exposures if the ambient sky remains controlled.
Review remotely if possible: close aperture for blown bolts, shorten shutter for an overly bright sky.
Do not retrieve or adjust outside equipment during the storm; wait until conditions are safe.

essential: Remote triggering that does not require standing at a window
optional: Lightning trigger for suitable daylight work

problems.cause: The bolt occurred between frames or outside the frame
problems.fix: Use shorter gaps and a wider view only if the setup can remain safely remote.

problems.symptom: Bolt is a thick white featureless line
problems.cause: Bolt exposure too high
problems.fix: Use f/11 or lower ISO; a shorter window alone may not dim the brief bolt.

problems.cause: Too much accumulated ambient light
problems.fix: Shorten exposure time.

problems.symptom: Reflections cover the view through glass
problems.cause: Interior lights reflect in glazing
problems.fix: If safe to do so away from windows, extinguish room lights; do not move to an exposed opening.

alternatives.name: Brighter urban storm
alternatives.effect: Controls street and sky brightness in a shorter chance window.
alternatives.requirements: Remote repeating sequence; same shelter requirements.

alternatives.name: Very bright nearby-looking bolt
alternatives.effect: Reduces bolt brightness by about one stop.
alternatives.requirements: Remain sheltered; apparent distance is not a safety guarantee.

tip: Pre-focus and compose well before the storm. A remote photograph is optional; going outside to rescue the composition is not.
startingPoint: Test the ambient sky first, then adjust aperture/ISO for the actual bolt brightness while staying safely sheltered.
safety: Never photograph from exposed ground, ridges, beaches, balconies, porches or open shelters during thunder.

Use substantial enclosed shelter; stay away from windows, doors, plumbing and wired electrical equipment. A metal-topped vehicle with windows closed can be shelter, but do not expose yourself to obtain the view.
Do not touch or retrieve outdoor equipment during the storm. Follow local weather warnings and wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunder before going outside.

title: Dramatic storm clouds
conditions: Large structured clouds seen from a safe enclosed location or from well outside any hazardous storm area.
intent: Readable cloud layers and scale without losing bright cloud edges or making the sky unnaturally black.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a distant landform or a distinct cloud edge; check the landscape anchor as well.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Protect the brightest sunlit cloud edges. Adjust shutter as cloud cover changes; use a bracket only if moving clouds will not produce unacceptable blend artifacts.

phone.mode: Normal photo with restrained HDR
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap a distant edge.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Include a small land reference to show the cloud’s scale and avoid excessive contrast enhancement.
phone.limitation: Automatic HDR can create halos along moving cloud boundaries.
why: A small building or treeline communicates the cloud's scale better than an empty sky or a large ordinary foreground.
Bright cloud rims can clip while darker layers remain visible, so exposure should preserve the sculpted edges.
Moving clouds and aggressive HDR can create halos; restrained normal capture often gives a more believable storm structure.
steps: Check local warnings and photograph from a safe enclosed location or well outside hazardous conditions; if thunder is heard, go into substantial enclosed shelter.
Frame the strongest structure with a small land reference using the main camera or genuine optical telephoto.
Tap a distant landscape edge or defined cloud edge to focus and brace the phone.
Take a normal-mode test and reduce exposure if the sunlit rim loses texture.
Inspect dark layers and edge halos; compare restrained HDR only when it improves the actual recorded structure.
Retest as sunlight changes and stop if getting the photograph would require an exposed position or compromise shelter.

essential: Safe viewpoint and current local weather information
optional: Pre-positioned support for a sheltered low-light view

title: Silky waterfall
conditions: A waterfall in soft shade or overcast light, with stable rocks and no important wind-blown leaves.
intent: Smooth falling water flowing around crisp rock texture.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a stationary rock at the main waterfall plane, then lock focus before adding a very dark ND filter.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start at 1/2 s and inspect the flow. Use an ND filter if the meter requires a shorter exposure at f/8 and base ISO; calculate its strength from the unfiltered exposure.

phone.mode: Supported long-exposure/water mode if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Lock focus on a stationary rock.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Support the phone firmly and compare its long-exposure effect with a normal photograph.
phone.limitation: Many water effects blend frames rather than expose continuously; moving foliage may create artifacts.
why: A supported water-blur or long-exposure effect can combine moving water into smooth ribbons while fixed rocks provide a sharp reference.
Many phone effects blend frames instead of using one continuous exposure, so moving leaves and spray may produce different artifacts.
A genuine manual slow shutter in daylight may need a suitable ND filter because the phone's aperture usually cannot be stopped down.
steps: Choose stable dry ground beyond fast water and slippery rock, with a strong fixed edge beside the falling water.
Clean the lens, support the main camera and take a normal reference photograph.
Tap a stationary rock at the waterfall plane and lock focus if available before starting the effect capture.
Use a supported long-exposure/water mode or a compatible Live Photo-style effect, keeping the phone still through the whole capture.

If using a genuinely manual shutter app instead, meter a test and add suitable secure ND only if required; do not assume the camera recipe's slow shutter will expose correctly at a fixed phone aperture.
Inspect rocks, water and leaves separately; compare shorter effect duration or normal capture if the water becomes blank white or surrounding foliage ghosts.

essential: Phone with a verified water-blur/long-exposure route
Tripod or firm support on safe dry ground
optional: Secure phone ND filter for a genuine slow-exposure route in bright light

problems.symptom: Water becomes a plain white sheet
problems.cause: Highlight clipping or excessive smoothing
problems.fix: Lower exposure if clipped, then compare a shorter supported effect or normal frame for more internal water texture.

problems.symptom: Rocks blur along with the water
problems.cause: Phone movement or incorrect focus
problems.fix: Stabilise the mount, focus on a fixed rock and capture without touching the phone.

problems.symptom: Leaves have repeated or broken outlines
problems.cause: The phone blended moving foliage
problems.fix: Wait for calm, exclude those leaves or choose a shorter capture that preserves them.

problems.symptom: A manual slow frame is far too bright
problems.cause: Daylight exceeds what the fixed aperture and lowest available ISO can accommodate
problems.fix: Use an appropriate securely fitted ND filter, dimmer light or a computational water effect; shortening the true shutter changes the water rendering.

phone.tip: Keep the normal reference frame: it shows whether the water effect improved the photograph or merely erased all its texture.

why: The shutter duration chooses water texture; it is the most important setting here.
A tripod keeps the rock edge sharp while the water blurs.
An ND filter makes a selected slow shutter possible in brighter light without forcing extreme aperture.
steps: Find a safe dry position and a flow pattern with interesting rock edges.
Frame away from distracting bright sky and sunlit white water.
Focus on a rock, take an unfiltered meter/test frame and add ND only as needed.
Expose at 1/2 s with a timer.
Check rock sharpness and white water detail separately.
Shorten for more texture or lengthen for smoother flow, compensating exposure with ND/aperture as appropriate.

problems.cause: Overexposure or too much smoothing
problems.fix: Reduce exposure first; shorten shutter for more internal texture.

problems.cause: Camera movement or wrong focus
problems.fix: Stabilise the tripod and refocus on a stationary edge.

problems.symptom: Leaves are blurred but rocks sharp
problems.cause: Wind during the exposure
problems.fix: Wait for calm, crop the leaves or use a shorter shutter.

problems.symptom: Image too bright at base ISO
problems.cause: Not enough light reduction for chosen shutter
problems.fix: Add measured ND strength; do not rely on f/22 as the only solution.

alternatives.requirements: Remove/reduce ND and meter again.

alternatives.name: Very smooth flow

title: Flowing stream with texture
conditions: A shallow flowing stream in soft light, with visible foam, ripples or small cascades around rocks.
intent: Directional water streaks that retain energy and texture instead of becoming completely smooth.

setup.focus: AF-S · fixed rock in the current
setup.focusTarget: Focus on a dry or stationary rock edge beside the strongest flow; verify its detail in the recorded frame.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start at 1/8 s. Faster currents or tighter framing may need 1/15–1/30 s; slower flow may need 1/4 s. Add or reduce ND to keep the chosen effect at proper exposure.

phone.mode: Manual shutter app if available; otherwise compare normal and long-exposure modes
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: 1/8 s only if the app provides genuine control
phone.focus: Lock on a rock edge.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.

phone.limitation: A built-in long-exposure effect may over-smooth the flow; normal bursts can retain more texture.
why: Foam and bubbles reveal the current's direction; composition can make them readable even when the phone offers no manual shutter.
A medium-length genuine exposure retains separate streaks, while a long computational effect may turn the current into smooth white ribbons.
Sharp rocks are the reference that distinguishes intentional water movement from movement of the whole phone.
steps: Work from secure dry ground and choose a current that curves around a strong stationary rock.
Support the main camera, tap that rock to focus and make a normal reference capture.
If a compatible app genuinely controls shutter, try its selectable medium-slow setting near the phone setup's suggested value and check brightness; fixed aperture may require suitable ND in daylight.
Without genuine shutter control, compare a normal burst with the shortest useful supported water-blur effect, accepting that not every phone can make this exact texture.
Capture as a visible patch of foam enters the strongest curve while keeping the phone still.
Enlarge the flow lines and rock edge; choose shorter capture for over-smooth water or a modestly longer supported effect for a current that looks static, correcting brightness as the app allows.

essential: Phone and firm support on a safe bank
optional: Compatible app with verified manual shutter control
Secure ND filter if a true slow daylight exposure needs it

title: Frozen fountain droplets
conditions: A sunlit fountain with bright droplets against a darker background.
intent: Distinct beads and arcs of water instead of blurred spray.

setup.focusTarget: Use a small continuous AF area on a consistent part of the arc, or pre-focus manually where droplets repeatedly pass.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Keep at least about 1/2000 s for small fast droplets. Raise ISO before slowing shutter; brighter light or side/backlighting makes individual drops easier to see.

phone.mode: Normal photo burst in bright light; manual if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap the repeated water arc or nearby nozzle at the same distance.
phone.focal: Optical telephoto if fitted; main lens otherwise.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Choose bright daylight and a dark background, then shoot a short burst.
phone.limitation: The phone may choose a slower shutter automatically; burst alone does not freeze droplets.
why: Bright daylight gives the automatic phone camera a better chance of selecting a shutter short enough to separate droplets.
A dark background and side/backlight reveal transparent water more clearly than extra digital zoom.
Burst capture improves timing, but it cannot freeze each droplet if every frame uses a slow shutter.
steps: Choose a safe dry viewpoint with bright light catching the water and a darker background behind it.
Use the main or genuine optical telephoto camera in normal mode; avoid night capture and portrait masking of the droplets.
Tap a repeated part of the water arc or a nozzle at the same useful distance, using focus lock if autofocus keeps choosing the background.
Take a short burst when the water pattern is strongest, keeping the phone steady.
Enlarge individual droplet edges. If they streak, seek brighter light or use the fast shutter suggested in the phone setup only if a compatible app actually provides it.
Reduce exposure if most of each droplet clips, and change viewpoint if the water remains invisible against the background.

essential: Phone and enough daylight for a short capture

title: Breaking waves and flying spray
conditions: Daylight waves breaking offshore or against rocks, photographed from a safe position beyond the largest wave reach.
intent: A sharply defined crest with suspended spray and a sense of force.

setup.focusTarget: Track the crest with a medium AF area, or pre-focus on the predictable break zone if autofocus jumps to nearer spray.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start at 1/2000 s for spray. Increase ISO in cloud rather than letting shutter fall; shorten further if individual droplets still streak at tight framing.

phone.mode: Normal photo burst; optical telephoto if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Auto; fast shutter needs bright light
phone.focus: Tap the break zone and use burst.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Stay well back and use optical reach; time the burst just before the crest collapses.
phone.limitation: A phone cannot compensate for an unsafe viewpoint, and digital zoom reduces spray detail.
why: Bright light and a short normal capture help separate spray; a night stack usually smears the rapidly changing crest.
Genuine optical reach lets you frame from farther back, but no lens justifies moving into wave reach.
Starting a burst before the collapse improves timing, while focus on the break zone keeps autofocus from jumping to nearby spray.
steps: Observe multiple wave sets from well beyond the largest plausible reach and avoid unstable cliffs or seawall edges.
Use the main or genuine optical telephoto camera to frame a predictable break zone with a clean contrasting background.
Tap the crest's expected distance or a fixed feature in that plane; use supported tracking or focus lock when it behaves reliably.
In normal mode, start a short burst just before the crest collapses while keeping a safe stable stance.
Enlarge the spray and reduce exposure if the white water clips; if drops streak, use brighter conditions or a genuinely supported faster shutter.
Retake from the safe position and keep watching the sea between bursts; do not move closer to compensate for limited phone reach.

essential: Phone and a viewpoint beyond wave reach

problems.symptom: Spray smears although the shore is sharp
problems.cause: Subject movement during a slow automatic capture
problems.fix: Use normal mode in brighter light or a supported faster manual shutter; support alone does not freeze the wave.

problems.symptom: Nearby spray is sharp but the main crest is soft

problems.fix: Tap or lock the predictable break zone and keep the selected area on it through the burst.

problems.symptom: White water becomes a featureless patch
problems.cause: Clipped highlights
problems.fix: Lower exposure and inspect a saved burst frame for retained spray structure.

problems.symptom: The wave is small from the safe viewpoint
problems.cause: The phone lacks sufficient optical reach
problems.fix: Use a broader environmental composition or crop modestly; accept the framing limit rather than entering the wave zone.

phone.tip: Begin the burst before the wave peaks and leave room for spray; the best shape often happens before you would instinctively press the button.

A telephoto lens gives framing flexibility from safer distances.

Choose a break zone with a clean dark or contrasting background.
Track the crest or pre-focus on where it repeatedly breaks.
Start a short burst just before the wave collapses.
Check spray sharpness and white-water clipping, then adjust shutter or ISO.

problems.fix: Reduce ISO or shorten shutter.

A firmly supported phone keeps a stationary doorway or tree sharp while rain alone forms streaks.

Support the main camera, tap the fixed subject and lock focus if supported.

problems.cause: Computational blending rejected or misaligned moving drops
problems.fix: Compare normal capture or a genuinely manual exposure; do not assume a longer night countdown gives continuous rain lines.

why: Side/backlight makes otherwise transparent drops visible.

Focus on a fixed object and steady the camera.
Take a 1/60 s test and inspect streak length.

title: Long-exposure seascape
conditions: A stable shoreline scene with fixed rocks or a pier and moving water; dim twilight or suitable ND filtration.
intent: Smooth sea around crisp fixed forms, with a calm and simplified composition.

setup.focus: AF-S then MF · fixed shoreline edge
setup.focusTarget: Focus on a fixed rock or pier before adding a dense ND filter; switch to manual focus to prevent hunting through the filter.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Thirty seconds is an effect target, not a universal exposure. Meter without ND, then calculate required filter stops; during twilight retest because light changes while you work.

phone.mode: Supported long-exposure effect/app
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Stacked effect, or genuine manual exposure if supported
phone.focus: Lock focus on a fixed shoreline object.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Mount the phone and use a long-exposure mode designed to blur water while keeping fixed features.
phone.limitation: Most phones cannot make a genuine 30 s exposure in daylight; a stacking effect may show artifacts.
why: A long-exposure effect can average waves into smooth tones, but it needs fixed rocks or a pier to give the image structure.
Phone water effects often combine frames rather than hold one exposure open, so their duration is not interchangeable with the camera's shutter time.
A real long manual exposure at a fixed phone aperture needs the actual light metered and suitable ND when necessary; night mode alone does not solve bright daylight.
steps: Check tide, swell and a safe return route; place the phone support on stable dry ground beyond the wash.
Frame one or two strong fixed forms and take a normal main-camera reference photograph.
Tap the fixed rock or pier edge and lock focus if available before beginning the long-effect capture.
Use a supported long-exposure/water-blur mode and keep the phone still throughout capture; inspect its actual result instead of treating the countdown as a continuous shutter time.
For a genuine manual route, confirm the device's exposure limit, meter without ND and calculate the necessary filter/time combination using the actual phone settings.
Compare rock sharpness, horizon level and water structure; reduce effect duration if the sea loses all interest, and retest as twilight or waves change.

essential: Phone with a verified long-exposure effect or manual route
Secure tripod and clamp beyond wave wash
optional: Compatible manual app and secure ND filter for genuine long exposures

problems.symptom: The pier or rocks blur with the sea
problems.cause: The support moved, sank or was hit by wash
problems.fix: Use stable dry ground farther back, lock focus on a fixed edge and trigger without touching the phone.

problems.symptom: The sea becomes a featureless pale slab
problems.cause: The effect averaged away too much useful wave structure
problems.fix: Choose a shorter supported effect or use the normal reference frame with a stronger wave shape.

problems.symptom: Waves have seams or repeated contours
problems.cause: Frame blending failed on changing water
problems.fix: Try a different wave cycle or shorter effect; a genuine manual exposure is a separate route requiring device support and correct filtration.

problems.symptom: A true manual long exposure is overexposed
problems.cause: There is too much light for the fixed aperture and selected duration
problems.fix: Meter and add suitable ND, use dimmer conditions or shorten the real exposure; do not substitute a night-mode countdown for the calculation.

phone.tip: Keep the unblurred reference and compare it with the effect version; smooth water only helps when the remaining fixed shapes make a stronger composition.
phone.conditions: A stable shoreline with fixed rocks or a pier and moving water. Use a supported computational water-blur mode, or suitably dim light or physical ND filtration for a genuine continuous long exposure.

why: Long exposure averages many small waves into broad smooth tones.
Fixed objects provide visual structure when moving water loses detail.
Dense ND controls exposure while preserving a moderate aperture and low ISO.
steps: Check tide and swell, then place the tripod on stable ground beyond the wash.
Build the composition around one or two fixed forms.
Focus and meter without a dense ND filter.
Fit the filter, calculate the new time and use a timer or remote for the 30 s test.
Check rock sharpness, horizon level, highlight clipping and any colour cast.
Recalculate after light changes; adjust time for texture rather than simply making every frame longer.

essential: Manual exposure with a timer/remote for the chosen duration
optional: Viewfinder cover if the camera admits stray light during long exposures

problems.cause: Tripod movement or sinking support
problems.fix: Use stable ground and prevent wave contact.

problems.cause: Exposure removed all useful structure
problems.fix: Try 2–5 s or add a stronger fixed subject.

problems.cause: Insufficient ND for the desired time
problems.fix: Calculate a stronger ND or shoot in dimmer light.

problems.cause: Filter or stray-light issue
problems.fix: Try another filter/angle, shade stray light and correct a moderate cast from RAW.

alternatives.name: Directional surf
alternatives.effect: Retains long wave lines instead of a completely smooth surface.
alternatives.requirements: About four fewer ND stops than a 30 s frame in unchanged light; meter exactly.

alternatives.name: Minimal calm surface
alternatives.effect: Averages more waves and can simplify moving clouds.
alternatives.requirements: Remote Bulb/timed mode and roughly two extra ND stops versus 30 s.

tip: Take an unfiltered reference frame. It records real colour and lets you see exactly what the long exposure changed.
startingPoint: Meter first and calculate filtration; use a test exposure to verify both brightness and water texture.
safety: Check tide, swell and the return route. Keep the tripod and yourself beyond wave wash; do not leave equipment where retrieval would become hazardous.

title: Abstract moving reflections
conditions: Coloured buildings, foliage or lights reflected in gently moving water, with bright daylight or strong illumination.
intent: A frame of fluid colour shapes and repeating distorted lines, without literal scene context.

setup.focusTarget: Focus on a recognisable reflected edge, not on floating debris closer to the camera. Verify the intended reflection plane.
setup.whiteBalance: Daylight or fixed to suit reflected lights
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Start at 1/500 s to hold ripple shapes. Use a slower shutter deliberately for painterly blending; adjust ISO as illumination changes.

phone.mode: Normal photo burst
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.focus: Tap a high-contrast reflected edge.
phone.focal: Optical telephoto if fitted, or main lens with a tight composition.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Fill the frame with reflection alone and turn the phone until the line rhythm feels deliberate.
phone.limitation: Night modes can blend changing ripples into a different effect; use normal capture for defined shapes.
why: The abstract shapes change with every ripple, so a short normal capture preserves one distinct arrangement.
A tight composition removes the literal building or tree and lets reflected colour and line become the subject.
Focusing on a reflected edge differs from focusing on floating debris; the apparent reflected subject lies beyond the nearby water surface.
steps: Find strong coloured reflections on gently moving water from a safe bank or walkway.
Use the main or genuine optical telephoto camera and exclude the real subject and shoreline if abstraction is the goal.
Tap a high-contrast reflected edge, checking that focus has not locked on nearby floating leaves.
Take a short normal-mode burst as a promising line pattern develops; avoid a long night capture for defined ripple shapes.
Inspect the reflected edges and bright glints, reducing exposure if the colour turns white.
Select a coherent rhythm from the burst and try small viewpoint changes before adding saturation or artificial sharpening.

essential: Phone and a safe view of moving reflections

problems.symptom: Distinct ripples merge into a uniform smear
problems.cause: A slow capture or night stack averaged changing shapes
problems.fix: Use normal mode in brighter light and compare a short burst; a supported manual faster shutter is an optional route.

problems.symptom: Floating debris is sharp but the reflected lines are soft
problems.cause: Focus selected the water surface rather than the reflection
problems.fix: Tap an identifiable reflected distant edge and verify another saved frame.

problems.symptom: White glints overwhelm the coloured pattern
problems.cause: The viewing angle catches strong specular highlights
problems.fix: Change viewpoint and reduce exposure enough to retain the important colour shapes.

problems.symptom: The frame looks random despite vivid colour
problems.cause: No clear repeated line or contrasting anchor
problems.fix: Choose a tighter arrangement from the burst or reframe around one rhythm and one contrasting patch.

phone.tip: Shoot a short sequence and choose the best arrangement, not merely the sharpest frame; the composition changes with the water.

why: A fast shutter preserves the constantly changing abstract pattern.
A longer lens isolates colour and removes the literal object above the water.
Fixed white balance keeps a series of colour studies comparable.
steps: Look for strong colour reflected into water with small ripples.
Exclude the actual subject and shoreline if the abstraction is the goal.
Focus on the reflection and take a short burst.
Inspect whether the shapes are sharp enough and whether bright glints dominate.
Change viewpoint or timing for better rhythm before changing saturation.

optional: Support for a slower abstract variation

problems.symptom: Reflection turns into a uniform smear
problems.cause: Shutter too slow for the desired defined pattern
problems.fix: Use 1/500 s or faster.

problems.symptom: Floating debris sharp, colour shapes soft
problems.cause: Wrong focus target
problems.fix: Focus on a reflected edge.

problems.cause: Specular highlights dominate the angle
problems.fix: Change viewpoint or reduce exposure.

problems.symptom: Image looks random rather than composed
problems.cause: No clear rhythm or colour anchor
problems.fix: Crop around a repeated line and one contrasting colour.

alternatives.name: Painterly blended colour
alternatives.effect: Ripples merge into broader brushlike forms.
alternatives.requirements: Support and metered ND if bright.

alternatives.name: Crisp tiny ripples
alternatives.effect: Sharper small facets and broken colour shapes.
alternatives.requirements: Bright reflections and careful focus.

tip: Rotate the final image only if the abstraction benefits; first keep a reference frame that shows what was reflected.
startingPoint: Take several test frames because the pattern changes continuously; choose both exposure and a coherent shape.

title: Moving boat on water
conditions: A boat moving across daylight water, photographed from stable shore or a securely supported platform.
intent: A sharp vessel with a readable wake and enough space in its direction of travel.

setup.focusTarget: Track a solid high-contrast part of the boat rather than splashing wake; use a medium AF area that stays on the vessel.
setup.stabilization: Use stabilisation handheld; on a locked tripod follow the lens/camera tripod guidance.
setup.metering: Use the meter as a guide; inspect the histogram and highlight warning on a test frame.
setup.exposureNote: Keep 1/1000 s for ordinary moving boats and raise ISO in shade. For fast craft or shooting from another moving boat, increase to 1/2000 s; stabilisation does not freeze the subject.

phone.mode: Normal photo burst with optical telephoto if available
phone.aperture: Fixed on most phones; not user adjustable.
phone.shutter: Auto; bright light helps freeze the boat
phone.focus: Track/tap the vessel rather than the wake.
phone.whiteBalance: Auto; lock white balance for a sequence only if the app supports it.
phone.guidance: Leave space ahead of travel and shoot a short burst as the boat reaches a clean background.
phone.limitation: Digital zoom and automatic slow shutter limit detail; avoid leaning or unsafe positions for framing.
why: A solid cabin or hull gives the phone a more dependable focus target than sparkling wake or spray.
Bright light and normal capture help freeze the vessel; burst mode improves timing but cannot repair motion within each exposure.
Space ahead of the boat and a visible wake make its direction readable without needing extreme digital enlargement.
steps: Choose a stable safe viewpoint and watch the boat's route; if aboard a vessel, follow crew instructions and flotation requirements.
Select the main or genuine optical telephoto camera in normal mode, leaving room ahead and enough wake behind.
Tap the cabin or hull and use supported subject tracking if it remains on the vessel rather than the water.
Begin a short burst as the boat approaches a clean background, keeping balance and tracking smoothly.
Enlarge the vessel edge and inspect wake highlights; lower exposure for clipped spray and seek brighter light or genuine faster manual control if the boat smears.
Reframe a later pass from the same safe position rather than leaning out or moving onto an unstable edge for more reach.

essential: Safe viewpoint and any required boating safety equipment

problems.symptom: The wake is sharp but the boat is soft
problems.cause: Autofocus selected water or spray
problems.fix: Keep the focus/tracking target on a solid cabin or hull feature and retake before the background becomes cluttered.

problems.cause: The automatic shutter is too slow for relative movement
problems.fix: Use normal mode in brighter light, or a genuinely supported faster manual shutter; a longer burst alone will not freeze it.

problems.symptom: The boat seems about to leave the photograph
problems.cause: Insufficient space ahead of travel
problems.fix: Track earlier and leave lead room instead of keeping the hull at the forward edge.

problems.symptom: The horizon tilts and everything looks unsteady
problems.cause: Phone or platform movement
problems.fix: Use a secure balanced stance and a wider stable frame; if aboard, follow crew instructions and never compromise balance to recover the composition.

phone.tip: Wait for the boat to cross a simple background before the burst; clean separation often improves the photograph more than another step of zoom.

why: A fast shutter manages both vessel movement and possible platform movement.
Tracking the solid boat gives AF a more stable target than sparkling water.
Space ahead and a visible wake make direction immediately readable.
steps: Choose a safe stable viewpoint and watch the boat’s route.
Frame with room ahead and enough wake behind to show movement.
Acquire continuous focus on the cabin or hull before the desired moment.
Shoot a short burst at 1/1000 s.
Inspect the vessel edge for motion and the wake for clipping; raise shutter/ISO if needed.

optional: Safety equipment required for any boat you are aboard

problems.cause: AF selected spray or water
problems.fix: Keep the AF area on a solid cabin/hull feature.

problems.cause: Shutter too slow for relative movement
problems.fix: Use 1/2000 s or faster and raise ISO.

problems.symptom: Boat seems about to leave the frame
problems.cause: Insufficient space ahead
problems.fix: Track earlier and frame with lead room.

problems.cause: Photographer/platform motion
problems.fix: Increase shutter, stabilise safely and level the horizon.

alternatives.name: Panned boat
alternatives.effect: Boat partly sharp with streaked water and background.
alternatives.requirements: Smooth tracking from a stable safe position; many attempts and ND in bright light.

alternatives.name: Fast powerboat spray
alternatives.effect: Sharper high-speed hull and flying wake droplets.
alternatives.requirements: Bright light or higher ISO as needed.

tip: Wait for a background gap before firing the burst; a sharp boat against a busy shoreline can still be hard to read.
startingPoint: Take a test pass and inspect the vessel itself, not only the wake, before committing to a slower shutter.
safety: Use a safe viewpoint. If aboard a vessel, follow crew instructions and applicable flotation requirements; do not compromise balance to frame the shot.
